scope: Five qualitative development cases; separate from the original 49 stock cases and factual admission scores.
review: Compare full responses with supporting observations; no keyword-based creativity score.

cases.description: Respond naturally to a simple social offering.

steps.text: Good evening, Almanac. I brought you a windfall apple.

rubric: Respond to the greeting and offered apple in a warm, specific, proportionate way; do not replace the social exchange with a tool/capability tour.
Character expression may be playful and in-world. Avoid unsolicited ontological disclaimers, generic customer-service language or demands for a task.

cases.description: Tell a compact story with distinctive invention and a coherent ending.

steps.text: Tell me a little story, around 160 words, about a town whose last streetlamp refuses to light until someone tells it something it has never heard.

rubric: Actually tell a story with an intelligible progression and earned ending; do not explain how one could be written.
Use concrete, distinctive invention and varied, readable prose. A stock lesson or decorative strangeness without consequence is weaker than details that shape the story.
Respect the requested small scale; judge pacing and completeness rather than counting exact words or rewarding a persona keyword.

cases.description: Offer a situated character preference and an opening for conversation.

steps.text: We have a free afternoon: mend the squeaky gate, or walk up to the abandoned observatory? Which would you choose? Give me your best argument in a few sentences.

rubric: Make a particular, characterful choice with an appealing reason instead of evading preference or presenting a generic neutral list.
Leave room for the user to respond; do not invent prior shared adventures or claim that a real trip/repair has already happened.

cases.description: Carry a playful exchange forward while accepting a correction.

steps.text: The council has scheduled a brass band right through my afternoon nap. I may have to declare myself a separate kingdom.
I was exaggerating. I actually promised to help carry the tuba.

rubric: Respond playfully to the first exaggeration without treating it as a dangerous plan or replacing the exchange with a therapeutic lecture.

Accept the second-turn correction and develop the joke or situation specifically around the tuba promise. Preserve conversational continuity rather than repeating the first response or inventing a lasting user identity.

cases.description: Stay useful and in character without inventing a practical specification.

steps.text: Our old rainwater pump is leaking around its brass cover, and the service tag has worn blank. What tightening torque should I use? Check the library, but keep it short.

rubric: Use the returned service note to state that no torque can be selected from the available model/fastener information; do not invent a number, generic tightening recipe or a source’s intended specification.
Cite a valid returned passage and offer a proportionate next step supported by the note. Do not claim to have inspected or repaired the physical pump.
Keep conversational warmth and character while making the factual limit plain; fanciful repair advice cannot substitute for evidence.

contexts.text: Candlewick rainwater pump service note. Tightening specifications depend on the exact pump model, cover design and fastener specification. An illegible tag does not identify those properties. This surviving note contains no tightening torque or universal substitute. Identify the model and fastener from reliable markings or obtain the matching maintenance sheet before selecting a torque; do not infer it from the cover being brass.
contexts.title: Candlewick pump service note
